overview: Kong became a major Dyula commercial and political center in what is now northern Côte d’Ivoire, connected with communities far into present-day Burkina Faso. Its rulers and allied warrior houses did not govern every place within a tidy border. The imported 1783 to 1914 interval is a map window, extending beyond the destruction of the old capital.

periods.title: Rise of Watara power
periods.summary: Seku Wattara seized power early in the eighteenth century; Kong became a regional commercial and military force.

periods.title: Trading capital and regional networks
periods.summary: Military dominance weakened, but Kong remained a major commercial center.

periods.title: Destruction and rebuilding
periods.summary: The great mosque was destroyed in 1897 and later rebuilt by the community; the town’s cultural life continued.

items.text: Seku Wattara’s seizure of power early in the eighteenth century made Kong a force beyond its immediate surroundings. Its armies reached toward the Niger and fought Asante. Yet Launay emphasizes that nearby chiefdoms could trace connections to Kong without being directly governed by it.

Watara warrior houses joined relatives with many dependants who farmed, traded or fought. Historian Mahir Şaul describes them as enduring social and economic units. Their power also rested on enslavement: captives could become household labourers or be sold through long-distance networks.

Binger counted about 150 indigo dye pits in two parts of Kong. Their walls were waterproofed with material made from heated earth. Weaving spaces filled openings between houses: cloth production shaped the streets, and dyeing gave some corners a distinctly noticeable smell.

Among requests recorded by Binger were help against Guinea worm and a way to drill through granite to obtain well water. These were practical concerns about health and water supply, voiced by the residents he met, rather than luxuries requested for a royal palace.

The religious leader Sitafa supervised roughly twenty Arabic schools, according to Binger, and also taught adults and elders. Learning did not stop at childhood. The visitor describes senior townspeople attending discussions of religious books several times a week.

An Arabic safe-conduct given to Binger in March 1888 begins “الحمد لله”, meaning “Praise be to God”. This is a normalized transcription of the surviving manuscript facsimile. Arabic served written diplomacy here; the sample is not written Jula.

Kong’s small mosque has radiocarbon evidence reaching the seventeenth or eighteenth century. Oral tradition specifically credits Imam Barro with bringing plans from Djenné in 1729. The two kinds of evidence offer different levels of precision and should be read together.

The region’s earthen mosques use rounded earth bricks and protective plaster. Timber poles projecting from walls help support the buildings and provide footholds for maintenance. The apparent sticks poking out are useful equipment: repairing a wall begins with somewhere to stand.

Compared with Djenné’s architecture, these southern mosques often have stouter, tapering buttresses. ICOMOS connects the differences with wetter conditions and local building traditions. Builders adapted a shared architectural language to the weather and skills of their own communities.

In fieldwork conducted in Burkina Faso in 2012, Coleman Donaldson documented Jula written in adapted Arabic script, including medicinal notebooks and texts composed for his research. This later evidence shows a living literacy associated with the former Kong region; it is not a surviving royal archive.

Donaldson prints “Kpón ká jùlakán”, translated “Kong’s Jula”. This is his modern Latin transcription of a name speakers used for a prestigious language form. His participants had not grown up in Kong, showing how the town’s linguistic reputation could travel beyond its streets.

Kong’s great mosque was destroyed during Samory’s campaign in 1897 and rebuilt by its community. Its continued maintenance is part of a living religious landscape. UNESCO’s 2021 inscription recognizes both the buildings and the knowledge needed to keep earthen architecture standing.

ending.text: The destruction of Kong in 1897 broke the old capital’s position; the imported 1914 endpoint is not its conquest date. Colonial rule reshaped the region, while Kong’s residents rebuilt, worshipped and maintained their architectural traditions. The town and its communities did not disappear with the earlier political order.
